sections.html: The Nile puffer fish, Tetraodon lineatus, was the very first puffer fish to receive a scientific name valid in today's sense, in 1758. The maximum length is a little over 40 cm.

Aquaristically, the Nile pufferfish has a very bad reputation. It is considered to be extremely biting and incompatible, but curious and playful, so that sooner or later every co-inhabitant gets to feel its extremely strong teeth, which remind of a parrot's beak and easily crack open every snail shell and every mussel shell. The keeper should also beware of being bitten by a Nile puffer fish, as this causes bleeding wounds.

Like all puffer fish, it is poisonous and must not be eaten, at least at certain times, or one risks fatal poisoning.

The Nile puffer fish in the trade do not come from the Nile, but from the Niger. The two rivers were connected just a few 10,000 years ago and have very similar fish fauna. In the meantime Nile puffers are also bred in Indonesia.
It is a predator and prefers to eat small fish. To catch them, the comparatively clumsy and slow puffer fish has to be tricky. Its teeth easily crack open snail and mussel shells.

There is hardly any aquarium fish that can match the Nile puffer fish in intelligence. Fascinating for the observer are also its independently moving eyes, with which it attentively observes everything inside and outside the aquarium.

In ancient Egypt there was a hieroglyph in the form of the puffer fish, used as a determinative that stood for "discontented". The puffer fish was called "Fahaka" or "Fahaqa", which was also a synonym of the Nile puffer fish used until the 1980s.
